title: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room has said he turned from "camp, friendly and
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room has said he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.One of the women told the jury at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday: "He was just dark and arrogant and performing - he was scary, he was demanding."The woman told police she met Brand before he was famous while attending the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She alleges he later raped her.The woman said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid she may be pregnant in the aftermath of the alleged attack.Before the alleged rape, the woman also said Brand made her take photos of him with his top off, which were shown to the jury.The jury were played a police interview with the woman recorded in 2023, when reporting the alleged crime, before she was called to the witness box on Thursday. The complainant said she and Brand had gone back to a hotel room. She told the police officer she thought Brand "was gay" when they met earlier and she didn't feel like he was "trying it on with her".The woman said she had been in the bathroom, but when she came out "he had like briefs on - and I was like taken aback and shocked. He was prancing around".The complainant alleged Brand told her: "Don't worry, that's how I am."She recalled thinking "what on earth have I got into" when, she claims, a shirtless Brand made her take photos of him before the alleged attack.She was heard telling the officer: "I'm reporting that Russell Brand did rape me."What I'm going to say now - then, I second guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal."Sorry... he raped me basically - I know that happened. I remember him touching my breasts a lot - while kissing my neck."During the video evidence, Brand watched the TV screen attached to the dock - rarely taking his eyes away. He appeared to be listening attentively and hardly moved his position throughout.Describing the alleged encounter, the woman later told the jury: "He was big, I felt threatened and he's half-naked... I didn't think at that point his intentions were good.""He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn't the [same] person I was chatting to."She added: "He just changed suddenly from this... camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like."The woman recounted to police how Brand acted "like Basil Fawlty when he does his goose steps" before the alleged rape.She told the officer: "I remember him being like an ostrich - like a bird because he was very leggy."I wasn't laughing, I just remember him jumping up and down being silly."The woman said after Brand left the room she was "just sitting there crying and I felt stupid," adding: "In that moment in time I was just shocked."At one point in the police interview, she cried while saying "this was something dirty that had happened".She said she "thought it was my fault", adding that she was "having nightmares" about the possibility of being pregnant.The complainant said she had delayed coming forward because she was worried it would impact her professional life. "I was told if you come out with this, your career is done," she said.Under cross-examination Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC put it to the complainant that when she first met Brand she welcomed his attention."I welcomed his company, not what followed," the woman replied.He then suggested that she fell under his spell and that she wanted to spend more time with him.The woman replied: "That's incorrect. I did not fall under his spell and I did not find him attractive. "Asked by the defence why she agreed to go back to the hotel room with Brand, she responded: "I'm telling you... I thought he was a gay man, very softly spoken, very effeminate."I felt safe – I felt sexually safe with him. He was very intelligent and that appealed to me, not in a sexual sense. "The woman became tearful a number of times while giving her evidence from the witness box.At one point the judge told the witness to "take a moment, catch your breath", after she became emotional.Brand's barrister later challenged the complainant about why she did not run back into the bathroom or leave the room when she realised Brand had removed some of his clothes.She replied: "What was I supposed to do? Hide in bathroom? Walk out the room? Walk past him? I had no phone, no reception, no idea where I was. Run into the night with him following me?"Referring to photographs she had taken of Brand, she said: "I took those photographs, he told me to take them, he was showing off, he was prancing around... I was scared... I couldn't fight him."I blame myself for allowing him back into my room," the woman said.She was also challenged by the defence barrister about why she didn't report her allegation about Brand to the police in Bournemouth.She said: "I didn't report it as I didn't want anyone to know. I didn't think anyone would believe me."The woman told the jury that after she says she was raped by Brand she blamed herself "in that moment"."I hate that I blamed myself, I shouldn't have to blame myself."She also told jurors: "I regret to this day the error in judgment thinking this man would not rape me.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant

title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
description: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, accord
body: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman. The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward. The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentous shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied. "NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients."This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected. The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it."The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said. "Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces. Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms. She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation. An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

schema.headline: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says

title: What we know about the criminal investigation into US congresswoman Ilhan Omar
description: Image source, Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has has represented Minnesota since 2018By
body: Image source, Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has has represented Minnesota since 2018ByBrandon DrenonUS government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation".The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya. Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved.What is Omar being investigated for? Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband.The Wall Street Journal reported that her mobile phone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized."This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time.Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports.Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship.Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams".US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures. Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.How did Omar obtain her citizenship? Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he had "no concerns" about her citizenship.Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000.According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18. If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately. Who is Omar's father? After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker. Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications. According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee".The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship.Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991."[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator." The BBC has contacted Omar for comment. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Homeland Security Investigations agents were seen outside Omar's home on 12 OctoberCan Omar be deported?The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected. According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration.Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is revoked. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process. This appears to be where the groundwork is being laid in the current investigation into Omar.What has Omar said? Trump has repeatedly suggested Omar should be deported, calling for her to "go back" to Somalia.At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd.After her home was searched, Omar wrote on X: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "I will not be silenced."Trump has said the investigation into her has "nothing to do with me". The timing of the federal probe has defied justice department precedent of not taking action against officials running for office this close to an election. The raid happened with the November midterm elections only weeks away, drawing condemnation from some of Omar's Democratic colleagues, who said she had been subject to relentless "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations".

schema.headline: What we know about the criminal investigation into US congresswoman Ilhan Omar

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
description: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.N
body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal."We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries". The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up. In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:The need for free expression of opinion in news mediaThe need for a range of views in news media across the UKThe need for a range of people controlling the media across the UKThe need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UKThe letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns. A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process."This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

schema.headline: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm

title: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?
description: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!",
body: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines."Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says."And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust.He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein."If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded.Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away."The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

schema.headline: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?

title: Katie Price 'coached' ex's alleged rape victim, court told
description: Image source, Press Association'Image caption, Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him BySara SmithReporting fromat Lewes Crown Court and Vic
body: Image source, Press Association'Image caption, Kieran Hayler denies all the charges against him BySara SmithReporting fromat Lewes Crown Court and Vicky CastleSouth EastKieran Hayler has told jurors he thought his ex-wife Katie Price was "coaching" a 13-year-old girl he is accused of raping after discovering messages she sent to the alleged victim.Hayler, 39, said he took photographs of messages on Price's phone in which she discussed claims that he fancied the girl and wrote: "I will make you a little star."Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault involving the teenager in West Sussex in 2016.Giving evidence on Thursday, the former stripper denied the allegations and said: "I believe they've been fabricated."He told the trial that "trust had gone on both sides" of his marriage to Price by mid-2013, and he admitted affairs with three other women during their relationship.He told jurors "I am attracted to older women" and that all his significant relationships had been with older women.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Kieran Hayler told the court Katie Price was also unfaithful during their relationshipHayler said Price was also unfaithful during their relationship.Asked by his defence barrister Arlette Piercy why he took pictures of the messages between Price and the complainant, he replied: "Because she made out that I fancied [the complainant]."I thought, 'this is a bit weird'."He said he accessed her phone the same way she had accessed his, by using his fingerprint.Asked about what this showed, he said: "The relationship is breaking down."The court previously heard that Price messaged the teenager saying she had heard that Hayler and the girl had kissed and he had "tried it on" with her, adding later: "I will make you a little star."Asked during her evidence about the phrase, Price said it was "a figure of speech".On Thursday, Hayler said: "Everyone can interpret it how they want, it's very pushy. It's a very strange comment to make."I thought she was coaching her into [saying] something she shouldn't."I didn't send them anywhere, I took a picture on my phone."He told the court he found the picture of the messages "recently" after taking his phones out of storage when moving home.He then sent them to his solicitor.Alternative chargesOn Thursday, he also pleaded not guilty to four alternative counts of sexual activity with a child following the close of the prosecution case.The charges were added to the indictment for the jury to consider as alternatives to the three rape counts and one count of sexual assault.Judge Mark van der Zwart told jurors the prosecution alleged the complainant was raped, while Hayler's case was that nothing sexual had happened between them.Hayler denies all the charges.The court previously heard Hayler had claimed Price had "launched a campaign" against him after their marriage broke down and that the allegations formed part of it.The couple were married at the time of the alleged offences before separating in 2018 and divorcing in 2021.The complainant first contacted the NSPCC in 2021 and the charity referred her to police.The trial continues.Additional reporting by the Press Association.Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk , external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Severe drought and hosepipe bans - is your area affected?
description: Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in fu
body: Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation."A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too.Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

schema.headline: Severe drought and hosepipe bans - is your area affected?

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more
description: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he rele
body: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all the documents and answers key questions.The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.Hours later, Fifa released a video statement from Infantino. He had declined to speak to or take questions from the media, including the BBC.In the Fifa video, he said: "First of all I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise project which led to many consequences."But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal and in no way a done deal, that actually intended to enable Fifa to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources."Infantino said he would answer questions in writing "in due course" following what he said had been a "constructive discussion" with "different opinions and points of view".Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced."One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said."I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing."I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them."It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize."The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate."That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change."Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology."Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added."What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released. Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened.  "Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said.Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023."I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added."We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel."This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms."Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues".Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed.BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat. Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card.Fifa's legal committee will review and update Fifa Council in December."What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt."Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room."The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed."When he puts other dignitaries in front of his 211 associations, then he's lost what football is about," Hewitt said."And that was said by a number of people, not just the Europeans."How the Peace Prize came to be awarded will be the subject of an investigation by the Fifa social committee which will report back in December. "They will consider, first of all, how the Peace Prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed," Hewitt said."That committee will report back to Council in December and then Council will make the decision based on its recommendation."Today there was a watershed moment where it's very clear in order to move forward, which we all want to do, we have to understand the past."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more

title: Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez apologises for outburst and fined
description: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has issued an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.After United's
body: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has issued an apology following his controversial remarks criticising the club's hierarchy.After United's Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday, Martinez said the club had left head coach Michael Carrick with an under-equipped squad.Following talks with United on Thursday, the Argentina centre-back released a statement."Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager," Martinez said in a social media post."It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday's game."Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity."The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise."It is understood Martinez has been formally punished for his outburst with a fine.Carrick will hold a news conference on Friday, prior to the game against Leeds United on Sunday (14:00 BST).He takes his side to Elland Road on the back of just two wins from nine games this season, placed 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games.Following the loss to Atletico, Martinez said he expected more investment in the Manchester United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".The 28-year-old later said he "spoke out of anger and frustration" in making those comments and that he had "belief in my team-mates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward".Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane, speaking on The Overlap podcast,, external described the situation at his former club as "a bit of a circus".Martinez's statement on Thursday added: "Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not help with that."I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition: bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve."With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together."It remains to be seen whether Carrick selects Martinez for the trip to Leeds.Nevertheless, there is understood to be significant doubt over his long-term future at Old Trafford.His current deal expires at the end of the season but the club have the option of extending it by 12 months.While the issue over his recent comments is now considered closed, the club are still to decide whether they want to trigger the contract option.

schema.headline: Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez apologises for outburst and fined

title: Hole in Neanderthal shoulder bone linked to ancient wooden spear
description: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.They say a 15mm hole fo
body: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology."The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy."It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation."The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest."I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

schema.headline: Hole in Neanderthal shoulder bone linked to ancient wooden spear

title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
description: "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that
body: "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said."For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train."The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France."There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers. Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel. "This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

title: William Chapman died from 'multiple traumatic injuries' in tiger attack, inquest hears
description: Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining mult
body: Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death."Park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended but confirmed his death at the scene.The senior coroner said her office was awaiting a more substantial report as to the extent of his injuries. South Yorkshire Police provided a number of witness statements from the public and staff who were at the wildlife park at the time, the hearing was told.Mundy instructed staff to contact Yorkshire Wildlife Park to ask them to keep any relevant CCTV and inform the coroner of any previous visits by Chapman to the park.After opening the inquest, which Chapman's family chose not to attend, on Thursday morning, Mundy adjourned proceedings until 18 March 2027.Speaking after the hearing, a neighbour of Chapman told the BBC he was "very polite and well-spoken" and a "lovely man".Josh, 24, who lived in the same building as Chapman, said: "He'd always have a laugh and a joke. He was quite well kept, he'd look after himself physically. He loved his F1, he'd talk for hours about his F1 if he could."Discussing the online comments and speculation in the aftermath of the incident, he said: "People didn't know him. If you don't know him, don't make a comment."The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation of the Yorkshire Wildlife Park.An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.What we know about wildlife park tiger attackMobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.The park would reopen on Friday for the first time since the fatal incident, a spokesperson confirmed.In a statement, they said that staff members' "heartfelt sympathies" remained with Chapman's family and loved ones. "The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff team and animals remain our highest priority," they added."As we welcome visitors back, we would ask everyone to be understanding and respectful towards our staff team, who have shown tremendous professionalism and dedication during an exceptionally difficult time. "We are providing specialist trauma support and ongoing care for those affected."We continue to assist South Yorkshire Police and other relevant agencies with their ongoing inquiries into the circumstances of this tragic incident."A park spokesperson previously said the rare Amur tiger involved, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.A health and safety investigation has also been launched by City of Doncaster Council.

schema.headline: William Chapman died from 'multiple traumatic injuries' in tiger attack, inquest hears

title: Professor shares 'most important thing to do' when someone is grieving
description: Image source, Jamie CurtisImage caption, Dr Lesel Dawson encourages bereaved people to talk about their feelings in order to cope with griefByMae Dava
body: Image source, Jamie CurtisImage caption, Dr Lesel Dawson encourages bereaved people to talk about their feelings in order to cope with griefByMae DavageChloe HarcombeWest of England and John DarvallBBC Radio BristolKnowing what to say or how to support someone after a bereavement can be difficult. Fear of saying the wrong thing or intruding at a sensitive time can leave people worried about getting it wrong and avoiding reaching out altogether.But Dr Lesel Dawson, from the University of Bristol, said this is the worst thing people can do.Speaking ahead of an annual Good Grief Festival that Dawson is co-director of, she said: "The most important thing when helping someone dealing with grief isn't what you say, but that you don't turn away."A simple acknowledgement like 'I'm so sorry and I'm here' can mean a great deal, and it's vital to let the grieving person lead - to follow their pace, their language and their need to talk about the person who died."The associate professor in Literature and Culture also said people avoiding dealing with their own grief can create lifelong challenges. Dawson's own understanding of grief was shaped by the stillbirth of her younger sister when she was eight years old and learning that for many years her mother blamed herself for the child's death."The way we avoid grief can be really harmful to us," Dawson said. "Being able to turn toward the pain of the experience is the only way we process what's happened."She said the lack of conversation about grief meant it took "a while" to fully grasp what had happened.Research commissioned by Marie Curie found , externalthat while 70% of people feel comfortable talking about death, far fewer have actually had those conversations with family, friends or healthcare professionals.Blame and guiltWhile her mother struggled to cope with the bereavement, Dawson found an interest in psychology and emotions.But after Dawson's first son was born at 29 weeks and suffered complications linked to the premature birth, the loss of her sister and the memory of her mother's "great pain" came to the forefront of her mind.When Dawson revisited the difficult topic of conversation with her mother after her own pregnancy experience, she realised that her mother "felt [the stillbirth] was her fault"."I said to her, 'was it my fault that my son was born early?' and she said, 'no of course not'. "I said, 'okay, why can you not show the same compassion to yourself and your own loss?'" Dawson told BBC Radio Bristol.She added that feelings of blame and guilt were "very common" during bereavement and could lead to "destructive" coping mechanisms."The biggest myth about grief is that it happens in neat, orderly stages and that you eventually get over it," said Dawson."In reality, grief is messy, unpredictable and deeply individual. People move back and forth between feelings, and the idea of a tidy, linear process simply doesn't reflect how grief actually works."Image source, Paul BlakemoreImage caption, Good Grief Weston offers workshops, talks and musical performances aimed to start and normalise conversations about lossFollowing her own experiences with grief, Dawson took up the role of co-director of Good Grief, a festival in Weston-super-Mare that aims to start and normalise conversations about death, dying and bereavement.The festival, which begins later, offers a number of workshops, music events, talks and light installations until Sunday."Grief involves lots of emotions, it involves sadness, but also anger, numbness, jealousy, rage… they're not sequential."Everybody's individual. We have our own ways of grieving and coping and we have our own timelines," Dawson said.If you or someone you know has been affected by the details raised in this story, advice on where to find help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Professor shares 'most important thing to do' when someone is grieving

title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings without public outcome, BBC Verify finds
description: ByMerlyn ThomasBBC Verify correspondent and Maryam AhmedBBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of kill
body: ByMerlyn ThomasBBC Verify correspondent and Maryam AhmedBBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.How does the IDF investigate incidents?The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", external, had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own"."That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments."[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".GazaSince the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.Image source, Latin Patriarchate of JerusalemImage caption, Nahida and Samar Anton were killed by Israeli troops in Gaza in December 2023BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."Deadly attack on school buildingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Palestinians inspect the destruction following the Israeli attack on the Al-Taba'een school building in August 2024 One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque.The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around.Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military.The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review.West BankImage source, ReutersImage caption, Women and girls mourn during the funeral of 16-year-old Palestinian Lujain Musleh in the occupied West Bank in September 2024BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law.More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, external. BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured.One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation.Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house.The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.LebanonImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The aftermarth of an Israeli strike in the town of Almat in November 2024BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon.The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities.One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children, near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry.Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review.Long running investigationsMichael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation".Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential."Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC),  said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded."She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate"."If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added.MethodologyBBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026.We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined".This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above.This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents.We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed.We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents.For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report.We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests.For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken.For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website.This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website.This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search.Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

schema.headline: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings without public outcome, BBC Verify finds

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
description: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previo
body: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die"."I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.  The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said. John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise"."It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan. "The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
